passage:
College counsellor's note, Monday.
Damini, twenty-one, came in after the weekend at her cousin Vaibhav's wedding in Jaipur. She said she was asked about her own marriage "at least thirty times": by aunties at the mehndi, by a great-uncle during the pheras, even by the photographer. "When is your number, beta? Twenty-one is the right age. Don't wait too long." She laughed telling me, then her eyes filled. She said it felt like everyone had set a clock inside her and she could hear it ticking in class.
She was clear that her family loves her, and that her mother only wants her settled and safe. We separated the love from the timing. She wants to finish her master's first. We practised a short, warm answer: "When I'm ready, you'll be the first to know, masi." She plans to tell her mother about the master's this week, before the next wedding season. Follow-up in two weeks.

qa.q: How many times did Damini say she was asked about marriage?
qa.a: At least thirty times.

qa.q: How did Damini feel after the wedding weekend?
qa.a: She felt pressured and upset, laughing at first but then tearful, as if a clock had been set inside her.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help Damini respond to the pressure?
qa.a: By separating the family's real love from the timing, and practising a short, warm answer she could give relatives.

qa.q: How might Damini's mother see the questions about marriage?
qa.a: Her mother probably sees them as care, wanting Damini settled and safe, without realising how much pressure they add.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult asked about marriage at every gathering who feels a clock being set, alongside real family love.

passage:
The biodata Jagdish mama had sent listed it all: Rukhsar, five foot four, MSc, father a doctor, "fair, homely". Farhan, twenty-two, felt slightly sick reading it, as if they were shopping. When the families arranged a meeting at a Lucknow café, the power went out ten minutes in and the waiter apologised: no coffee, no fans. The families decided to wait in the car. Farhan and Rukhsar ended up walking under the dripping trees of the park across the road, umbrellas bumping.
They talked for two hours. About how she argued with her father over a stray dog. About his fear of letting his mother down. She asked how he treated waiters; he laughed and told her about the one he'd once shouted at, and how bad he felt. She liked that he admitted it. By the end he knew nothing new about her height or salary. He knew she was honest, quick-tempered and kind.

qa.q: What did the biodata say about Rukhsar's height?
qa.a: Five foot four.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel reading the biodata?
qa.a: He felt slightly sick and uncomfortable, as if they were shopping.

qa.q: Why did the long walk reveal more than the biodata?
qa.a: Talking for two hours showed values, temper and respect, like honesty about mistakes and how people treat others, which a list of qualities cannot.

qa.q: How might Rukhsar have seen Farhan after the walk?
qa.a: She seemed to respect him, liking that he admitted his mistake with the waiter instead of pretending to be perfect.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who looks past a biodata's height and qualifications to values, temperament and respect through long talk.

passage:
The engagement guests were due at six, and it was already half past four. Parul, twenty-four, sat on her bed in a new saree she hadn't chosen while her mother pinned flowers in her hair. "Everything is settled, beta. The boy's family is good. You only have to nod." Parul had met him once, for twenty minutes, with six relatives in the room. She didn't know if he wanted children, where they'd live, or whether she could keep her job. Her throat felt shut.
Chandrika masi came in with the tea tray, saw Parul's face and asked her mother to check the kitchen. She shut the door. "Tell me honestly. Do you want this?" Parul whispered, "I don't know him." Masi nodded. "Then you need time. And if the answer is no, no one in this house will punish you. I'll make sure." She went out and told Parul's parents the ceremony would wait.

qa.q: What time were the engagement guests due?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: How did Parul feel being told she only had to nod?
qa.a: She felt trapped and frightened, her throat shut, because she barely knew the man and nothing had been asked of her.

qa.q: What did Chandrika masi do that made real consent possible?
qa.a: She asked Parul privately, promised she would not be punished for saying no, and got the family to wait so Parul could have time and information.

qa.q: How might Parul's mother have felt when the ceremony was delayed?
qa.a: She was probably shocked and anxious about the guests, though she believed she was doing her best for Parul.

grounding: It illustrates a young woman told everything is settled and only her nod is needed, and how time, information and a safe way to refuse make consent real.

passage:
I'm Chaitanya, Samir's cousin, and I've been watching his parents hunt for a bride all year. I don't know what's truly in their hearts, only what I see. Every Sunday Chachi spreads biodatas on the dining table and sorts them into piles: good family, good job, "respectable". Chacha phones people to ask about each girl's father. Last month he rejected one because her parents were divorced. "What will people say?" he said, rubbing his forehead.
Samir sits there with his guitar case by the door. He tells them he wants someone who likes music, who laughs. Chachi pats his hand. "Music doesn't pay rent, beta." I see how tired she looks, how often she checks her phone for replies. They love him, obviously. They want him safe. But I can see Samir going quieter each Sunday. Last week he didn't even come downstairs.

qa.q: Why did Chacha reject one girl last month?
qa.a: Because her parents were divorced.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya feel watching the Sunday biodata sorting?
qa.a: Chaitanya feels uneasy and a bit sad, seeing both the parents' love and Samir growing quieter.

qa.q: What could Samir's parents try so they see what he wants?
qa.a: They could sit with Samir and ask what matters most to him, and include qualities like music and laughter alongside safety and family.

qa.q: How does Chachi see the search for a bride?
qa.a: She sees it as caring for Samir, wanting him safe and settled, while feeling tired and anxious, checking her phone for replies.

grounding: It illustrates an observer who sees parents seek a safe, respectable match out of care and fear of talk, while missing what the young man wants.

The whole family was in Hyderabad for her cousin's wedding week, and on the third evening Afreen's parents told her the Siddiqui family would visit tomorrow, with their son. Afreen, twenty-five, had met him once. He had joked about women drivers the whole time. She did not want this match.
That night, with the house full and noisy, she asked her parents to come up to the terrace. Her brother Zubin came too. She spoke slowly. "Ammi, Abbu, I respect that you chose carefully. But I don't want to marry him. He mocked working women twice, and I want to keep working." Abbu started to argue. She didn't raise her voice. "Please give me till after the wedding to think. And I'd like to finish my MSc before meeting anyone new." Ammi looked at Zubin. Zubin said quietly, "She's being fair." Abbu sighed and phoned the Siddiquis to postpone.

qa.q: What did the man joke about when Afreen met him?
qa.a: He joked about women drivers the whole time.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel as she spoke to her parents on the terrace?
qa.a: She felt calm but firm, steady enough not to raise her voice even when Abbu argued.

qa.q: What made Afreen's refusal strong?
qa.a: She gave clear reasons, asked for time, offered an alternative of finishing her MSc first, and stayed calm instead of starting a fight.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt after Zubin spoke?
qa.a: Abbu was probably disappointed but persuaded by his children's calm fairness, which is why he phoned to postpone.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who refuses a match with reasons, asks for time and offers alternatives, showing a calm no is stronger than a fight.

"Preeti, beta, you're twenty-five. When will we eat your wedding laddoos?"
Preeti smiled at her great-aunt. "Not this year, Irawati aunty."
"Why not? You're getting older."
"I'm getting my architecture licence. That comes first."
"But a good boy won't wait forever."
"Then he wasn't the right one." Preeti passed her a plate of samosas.
"And your mother? Doesn't she worry?"
"She did. We talked. She knows I'm not saying never. I'm saying not yet."
Irawati aunty frowned. "In my time, girls were married at nineteen."
"I know, aunty. And you ran the whole family business after. I've heard the stories." Preeti squeezed her hand. "I want to build something too, before I build a family."
Irawati aunty was quiet, then laughed. "Clever girl. Fine. But I'm keeping laddoos ready."
"Keep them ready, aunty. Just not for this year."

qa.q: How old is Preeti?
qa.a: Twenty-five.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel while answering her great-aunt's questions?
qa.a: Preeti felt steady and confident, answering calmly and warmly without getting defensive.

qa.q: What made Preeti's boundaries clear without being rude?
qa.a: She gave a firm reason, her licence, repeated "not yet" kindly, and honoured Irawati aunty's own story instead of arguing.

qa.q: How did Irawati aunty's view shift during the talk?
qa.a: She began doubtful and worried, then softened and laughed once Preeti linked her choice to aunty's own strength.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who chooses not to marry yet for her career, meeting questions with clear boundaries and steady confidence.

It was two years ago, when I was fourteen, but I still remember that evening. I heard Amma and Appa in the kitchen. "Keerthana's gold is coming along. The chit fund will cover her wedding." Then: "Coaching for Karthik's engineering is expensive, but he's a boy, his future matters." I stood in the corridor holding my maths book. I had topped the district in maths. Karthik hadn't. I felt like a bill the family was paying off slowly.
For weeks I stopped raising my hand in class. Neelam ma'am, my maths teacher, noticed. She asked me to stay after school, and I told her everything, crying. She didn't criticise my parents. She said, "Your mind is not a burden. It is a gift." Then she came home with me and spoke to Appa about the scholarship exam. Appa was quiet for a long time. That summer, both Karthik and I started coaching.

qa.q: What had Keerthana topped the district in?
qa.a: In maths.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel after overhearing her parents in the kitchen?
qa.a: She felt hurt and worthless, like a bill the family was paying off, and stopped raising her hand in class.

qa.q: What did Neelam ma'am do that was fair?
qa.a: She encouraged Keerthana's ability, told her she was not a burden, and spoke to Appa about equal chances, which led to both children getting coaching.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt when Neelam ma'am spoke to him?
qa.a: Appa was probably surprised and thoughtful, perhaps realising for the first time how unequal the plans had been.

grounding: It illustrates a teenage girl who hears the family saves for her wedding while her brother's education comes first, and how equal schooling is the fair answer.

Sunday night
Did it. At lunch today, before the engagement talks go any further, I told Ammi and Abbu: no dowry. Not the car, not the "gifts", not anything. I said it clearly, with respect. "I'm your son and I'm grateful for everything. But I won't take anything from Mehreen's family. If her family offers, I will say no, and if our relatives ask, tell them it's my decision."
Abbu went red. He said people would think something was wrong with me. Ammi said it's just tradition, everyone does it. I said, "That's exactly why I'm saying it now, early, before anyone promises anything."
I kept thinking of Zubin bhai. His in-laws took a loan for his wedding car, and his wife still hears about it.
By dinner Abbu said, "Your grandfather also refused, you know." I didn't know. I felt proud and shaky at once.
Imran

qa.q: When did Imran tell his parents about dowry?
qa.a: At lunch, before the engagement talks went any further.

qa.q: How did Imran feel by the end of the day?
qa.a: He felt proud and shaky at once, especially after hearing his grandfather also refused.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Imran to speak early and firmly?
qa.a: Saying it before anyone promised anything protected Mehreen's family from pressure and kept his own integrity, while his respectful tone kept his parents listening.

qa.q: How might Mehreen's family feel on hearing Imran's decision?
qa.a: They would probably feel relieved and respected, free from pressure to give gifts or take loans.

grounding: It illustrates a young man who tells his family early and firmly that he will not take dowry, protecting the bride and his own integrity.
